articles.title: Your checkout works. That's exactly why the real bug hides.
articles.excerpt: A reviewer on a GitHub discussion found a real hole in a diagnostic tool, and the exchange is a better teaching case than most of what gets written about pricing on purpose. The tool is a five-questio…
articles.body: A reviewer on a GitHub discussion found a real hole in a diagnostic tool, and the exchange is a better teaching case than most of what gets written about pricing on purpose. The tool is a five-question classifier: ask whether a product has traffic, whether visitors activate, whether checkout works, and so on, stop at the first "no," and file the failure under one of four modes (traffic, activation, billing, positioning). The reviewer, chenhz01 , pointed out that symptom-based classifiers like this tend to confuse adjacent failure modes: a billing failure can look exactly like an activation failure from the outside, so a single-label verdict throws away information a ranked list would have kept. That's a fair general critique, and it mostly doesn't apply here.

articles.title: WooCommerce Cart Session Performance Issues
articles.excerpt: I’ve audited and rebuilt a lot of WooCommerce sites, and the same pattern shows up on nearly all of them: the site benchmarks fast, real shoppers experience it slow, and the performance audit the owne…
articles.body: I’ve audited and rebuilt a lot of WooCommerce sites, and the same pattern shows up on nearly all of them: the site benchmarks fast, real shoppers experience it slow, and the performance audit the owner paid for never mentions why. The culprit is WooCommerce’s cart session handling, which quietly disables page caching for exactly the visitors who matter most, the ones with something in their cart. Based on the feedback I’ve gotten over the years, this rarely comes up in WooCommerce performance audits. It should be the first thing checked.

articles.title: Building a Pre-Trade Microstructure Risk Gate in Python: Hysteresis, EWMA Spikes and Taker-Sweep Detection
articles.excerpt: The research parts of this series ended in the same place: the signals that matter are about timing, and the most useful one was the bluntest. In Part 5's two-week capture, a single large Binance take…
articles.body: The research parts of this series ended in the same place: the signals that matter are about timing , and the most useful one was the bluntest. In Part 5's two-week capture, a single large Binance taker sweep warned of Polymarket repricing better than VPIN or book imbalance did, and pausing after sweeps was the only trigger that clearly beat randomly timed pauses (on BTC). This part is engineering, not research. It builds the thing most trading bots actually need: a pre-trade gate . Before every order, ask "is the book around this symbol in a state I shouldn't trade into?", get a yes or no with reasons, and fail closed when you can't tell. No streaming infrastructure, no event loop, about 120 lines of Python on followsm-sdk . TL;DR Reuse your HTTPS connection.

articles.title: Letting a coding agent use SSH without giving it your key
articles.excerpt: When a coding agent needs to reach a server, the easy options are both bad. You can leave a key where the agent can read it, or you can tell it to use your normal ssh setup and hope it only does what…
articles.body: When a coding agent needs to reach a server, the easy options are both bad. You can leave a key where the agent can read it, or you can tell it to use your normal ssh setup and hope it only does what you meant. I build Styx, a free and open-source desktop app that runs coding agents and makes them ask before they touch production. This is how it handles SSH, what the agent actually gets, and where the protection ends. A target, not a key An SSH target in Styx is a host, a user, a port (22 by default), an optional jump host ( user@bastion:22 , comma-separated for several) and an environment: prod, staging or preview. Agents don't get a special tool. They run plain ssh <host> , scp , sftp or rsync , and Styx applies the target's user, port and jump host for them.

articles.title: HubSpot Tracking & Consent Mode v2 Attribution Issues
articles.excerpt: Google Consent Mode v2 changed how Google’s own tags behave when consent is denied: they keep firing, but strip identifiers and send cookieless pings that Google models into estimated conversions. Hub…
articles.body: Google Consent Mode v2 changed how Google’s own tags behave when consent is denied: they keep firing, but strip identifiers and send cookieless pings that Google models into estimated conversions. HubSpot has no equivalent mechanism. Its tracking code either runs and sets cookies or it does not run at all, and nothing in Consent Mode tells it what to do. That mismatch is where the reporting goes wrong. This is the failure I see most often in audits, and it is invisible until someone asks why two systems disagree. Consent Mode v2 Does Not Govern HubSpot The most common misunderstanding is that Consent Mode is a site-wide consent system. It is not. It is a Google-specific signalling layer that adjusts the behavior of Google tags: Google Analytics, Google Ads, Floodlight.

articles.title: Subagents and the iron triangle: when fanning out costs more than it saves
articles.excerpt: Spawning subagents is the feature everyone wants to show off. Hand the model a big task, split it into five, run them at once, done in a fifth of the time. On a demo it looks like free speed. It is no…
articles.body: Spawning subagents is the feature everyone wants to show off. Hand the model a big task, split it into five, run them at once, done in a fifth of the time. On a demo it looks like free speed. It is not free. It is the old project triangle — speed, cost, quality: pick two — wearing new clothes. Subagents buy you speed. The bill lands on the other two corners, and whether the trade is worth it depends entirely on one property of the work: does it share state. What fan-out actually costs Run five agents instead of one and you pay in two places that do not show up until later. Cost. Each agent carries its own context and burns its own tokens. Five agents reading the same repo is roughly five times the input, not one fifth.

articles.excerpt: What Oracle and Xerox Do Not Say About CVE-2026-21932 Overview CVE-2026-21932 has enough public detail to support patching and inventory work. It does not have enough detail to support a precise explo…
articles.body: What Oracle and Xerox Do Not Say About CVE-2026-21932 Overview CVE-2026-21932 has enough public detail to support patching and inventory work. It does not have enough detail to support a precise exploit narrative for Xerox FreeFlow. The useful analysis is the boundary between confirmed vendor facts and reasonable uncertainty. Confirmed facts Oracle published the CVE in the January 2026 Critical Patch Update on January 20, 2026. The issue is in AWT and JavaFX and affects Java SE, GraalVM for JDK and GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Oracle lists these affected Java SE versions: 8u471 8u471-b50 8u471-perf 11.0.29 17.0.17 21.0.9 25.0.1 The GraalVM entries are 17.0.17 and 21.0.9 for GraalVM for JDK, and 21.3.16 for GraalVM Enterprise Edition. The CVSS 3.1 score is 7.4.

articles.title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
articles.excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new…
articles.body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal. Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions.

articles.body: NASA's Artemis IV moon mission will be a complicated affair — especially if SpaceX's Starship ends up being the lunar lander. For all of the changing components of the Artemis program over the past several years, one of its most persistent may be the question of how many refueling flights Starship will need to land astronauts on the moon . By summer 2021, it was common knowledge that Starship would require multiple launches to pull off an Artemis moon landing. A Government Accountability Office audit at the time, for example, estimated that it could take up to 16. Earlier this month, a member of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel said the refueling number could be as high as 22.

articles.body: "Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966. There were a bunch of Trekkie-themed celebrations and news stories over September, including festive documentaries , special screenings , tributes, parade floats , interviews, and even a Galileo shuttle story. Now, publishers Penguin Random House and Ten Speed Press are releasing " Star Trek: The Original Voyages: A Visual History " on Nov. 10, 2026. This coffee table book promises unprecedented exploration of the pioneering space fantasy television series and enduring pop culture property that bolstered the space race and ignited sci-fi audiences' imaginations by taking us to strange new worlds and civilizations in the final frontier.
